Location.text: Jes Cafe and Darbast Platform (Mohsen Gallery), Tehran
Location.venue: Jes Cafe and Darbast Platform (Mohsen Gallery)

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Daab was an interactive performance formed over the course of six months in a participatory process, during the non-competitive section of "New Voices Theater Festival". This festival was dedicated to the youth aged 15 to 25 and is inspired by Noel Greig's methods in intercultural artistic exchange. In the festival's structure, each participant group was paired with another group and took part in several stages of exchanges and dialogues; a process that was going to lead to an independent performance at the end reflecting the process itself.

The "Phoenix youth theater group" was formed with 11 young participants, mostly students or university freshmen. During the initial months of the project some changes took place: Five members withdrew or were voted out by the rest of the group. The initial gender composition included seven girls and three boys. Two of the female members left in the first month, and later, the five girls of the group demanded to end collaboration with the three male members. In the final weeks, another boy joined the group as an auxiliary actor. In the final weeks before the public performance, the group lacked a unified thematic line or shared language.

The pressure to present a performance in such circumstances had created a feeling of failure and a dead end. In response to this situation, the group decided that in addition to the content of their work, the festival's structure and the internal dynamics of the group should also be critically examined. This rethinking became the conceptual foundation of the Daab performance; a word that refers to habit, custom, and disposition. The final performance consisted of the narrative of six youths who have gathered in the format of a talent show to create a collective work. The competitive aspect of this process gradually creates a rift between them and leads to the termination of the collaboration contract. At a moment before collapse, one of the performers stops the narrative and invites the audience to intervene to find a solution. Thus, the boundary between performance and a creation process becomes blurred.
Group Members: Mahsa Mohammad Asghari, Yasaman Ardabili, Nika Seyyedi, Ava Faghihi, Helia Mirshekar, Farshid Rashidi

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The performance as a "drama of process" did not start from a pre-written text or play, but rather was formed from group exercises, improvisation, and exchange with the paired group in the festival. Weekly 3 to 4 hour rehearsals initially took place in a rented rehearsal room, but due to financial and time constraints, some rehearsals were moved to public spaces like the Laleh Park open-air amphitheater. After the initial version was ready, the performance was first staged at Jess Cafe as a semi-public and semi private space to measure the quality of interaction with the audience and reduce the fear of official performance on stage. Then the final version was presented at Darbast Platform, within the framework of the festival. The project took shape in three spatial levels: 1- Rehearsal Spaces (Rehearsal Room and Park) 2- Cafe place in the city as a testing ground 3- Festival Venue as the official presentation setting. The stage layout was designed in a circular shape; actors in the center and the audience sitting in a ring around them. This layout reduced the physical and symbolic distance, allowed for improvisation tailored to the crowd's reaction, and also made the audience's bodies part of the visual fabric of the stage.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: The project was the first formal and serious experience of the supervisor as an artist/educator/facilitator of creative processes. The core idea was based on the belief that "theater is a rehearsal for life" and the participatory process of making theater can act like a "microcosm"; a space for practicing alternative ways of being together and experimenting with other forms of power structure and care in a safe environment. At the beginning of each rehearsal, the phrase "every rehearsal is a performance, every performance is a rehearsal" was repeated. The project sought to show how teenagers aged 15 to 20, when faced with competitive and hierarchical structures, can learn a common language and the experience of participation through art, and construct a different narrative of group work. The goal was to create critical and questioning art without assuming the position of an omniscient narrator and without transmitting a direct message. An equal relationship with the spectators was intended, in which the issue is put up for discussion, rather than providing a predetermined answer.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The most important challenge was the internal dynamics of the group and how male and female teenagers confronted each other. The separation of members and conflicts related to psychological safety determined part of the project's formation path. School pressure and the volume of homework limited the possibility of regular, multi-day rehearsals, and the process was practically reduced to weekly sessions. In terms of official oversight, due to the more informal framework of the festival and cafe performance, the project did not face direct censorship; however, a rap performance by one of the girls and dancing scene raised some internal concerns and affected the group's perception of risk-taking. In the face of limitations, the project's approach was to turn the limitation into part of the working method. The phrase "the performer must go on" replaced "the show must go on," and the health condition and chance to learn for each individual were prioritized over the success of the final product/output. Instead of producing an expensive play, the focus was placed on bodies, voices, and lived experiences. Stage design and props were designed with minimal resources: gouache containers, glue, colored paper, and the actors' personal clothes. The conflicts and fragility of group work also became the subject of the performance; both at the process level and the way the moment of the collapse, and breach of the contract is narrated which leads to the scene where they invite the audience to find a solution.

sections.title: Fundings & Partners
paragraphs: In collaboration with New Voices Theater Festival, 84 Theater Group, Mohsen Gallery, Darbast Platform, Jes Cafe.

The cost of renting the rehearsal studio was divided among the group members. The families of the teenage members were the main sponsors of the project. The revenue from ticket sales at the cafe Jes was split, 50% going to the cafe and the other 50% divided equally among the group members.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: Navid Ghavidel is an artist, facilitator, and designer of participatory processes based in Rasht. He holds a Master's degree in the Philosophy of Art from the Tehran University of Art. His work resides at the intersection of theatre, arts pedagogy, documentary, and dialogue-driven, collective methods of creation. In his projects, art is not merely a tool for producing a performance, but a platform for collective learning, rethinking relationships, and experimenting with alternative forms of "being together."

A significant portion of his work involves teenagers and marginalized groups, focusing on the connection between social imagination, care, collective agency, and the critical re-reading of power. In projects such as Daab, Manam-Bazi, Safe Zone, Ham-Ghesseh, Passing the Role, Live Archive, Mapping an Imminent Archive, Undercurrents of Partnership, and Ham-Risheh, Ghavidel employs a combination of performance, improvisation, narrative, collective writing, archiving, and fieldwork. He uses these to create situations where lived experience, memory, conflict, and participation are transformed into artistic material. Rather than focusing on a "final product" in the traditional sense, his focus is on the processes through which the relationship between art, education, institutions, and social life can be questioned. Consequently, his projects typically offer opportunities for dialogue, intervention, and collective reflection instead of providing definitive answers.

Phoenix Theatre Group was a collective of teenagers and young adults supervised by Navid Ghavidel. It operated through the collective participation of its members from March 2019 to September 2019 (Esfand 1397 to Shahrivar 1398). Most members had met in theatre classes at the Arasbaran Cultural Center and had practiced together for about a year before Phoenix was officially formed. The group's path was defined by group exercises, improvisation, dialogue, and collective creation. Their core philosophy during that period was "theatre is a rehearsal for life," meaning the collective process of making theatre is not just about a final performance, but an opportunity to test alternative forms of relationship, decision-making, care, conflict, and togetherness. The group's most significant experience was the Daab project-an interactive performance developed over several months for the "New Voices" festival. Their work did not start from a pre-written script; instead, it evolved through practice, exchange, trial and error, and confronting the group's internal tensions and deadlocks. Through this journey, Phoenix understood and practiced theatre not just as an artistic output, but as a space for experiencing collective labor, rethinking relationships, and testing participatory modes of performance.

subsections.title: A) Within the group
paragraphs: The process of producing the work was based on devised drama; without a pre-written text and without hierarchical directing. Group members proposed and reviewed themes and scenes through games, theater exercises, improvisation, and dialogue. The members of the two paired groups in the festival also engaged in creative exchanges and drew inspiration from each other's viewpoints. The group supervisor's role included forming the group, artistic training, acting as a liaison between the group and the festival's executive team, and facilitating internal dynamics without becoming a director in the traditional sense. As the process progressed, this role shifted closer to artistic curation.

subsections.title: B) At the performance level
paragraphs: The roughly 40-minute performance, initially kicks off with a confrontational phase. Then, one of the actors would stop the performance and ask the audience to enter the stage to find alternative ways to face the issue or to offer suggestions. Spectators could enter the stage in place of any character and play their role differently, or simply provide their perspective and feedback. Participation was entirely optional. To prepare for this intervention, short interactive situations were designed throughout the performance; including asking for financial help to buy art supplies or inviting a few spectators to participate in a theatrical contest. Project participants were diverse including: group members, supervisor, a writer who was added at the end of the project, festival organizers, other youth theater groups present at the festival, students' families as financial supporters, and the audience of each performance.
